messages.author: 4b681bcd9d4d425d
messages.subject: Suggestions re:Hard or Soft Constraints and using Narrow Ranges (for an ODE)?
parts:
Hi all,

I'm working with an ODE model, and I'm getting some errors that I think indicate I'm doing something non-optimal. (I realized that my previous question wasn't about what I was actually doing wrong - instead...)

Basically, my initial states for the ODE virus model are uncertain, as are some of the parameters. The state is a vector of people in 4 categories, S, E, I, or R. To create my initial values, I was doing something like the following; (This is NOT the full model, obviously, just the relevant parts for this question.)

model {
//My ODE SEIR Model
}

parameters {
  real<lower=0, upper=1> PCT_nonsuscept;
  real<lower=0, upper=1> PCT_Initial;
}

transformed parameters {
          real<lower=0> y0_vector[4];
          real y[N_t,4];

 y0_vector[1] <- (1-PCT_nonsuscept-PCT_Initial)*pop_sizes[g];
  y0_vector[2] <- 0;
 y0_vector[3] <- (PCT_Initial*pop_size;
 y0_vector[4] <- PCT_nonsuscept*pop_size;

          y <- integrate_ode(SEIR_Model, y0_vector, t0, t, theta, x_r, x_i);
}

model {
  PCT_nonsuscept ~ beta(500,200);
  PCT_Initial ~ beta(1,1000000);
}


I could be constraining these parameters, (instead of just centering them), to avoid getting errors about y0 being negative. 

My initial idea is to use;
  real<lower=0, upper=0.95> PCT_nonsuscept;
  real<lower=0, upper=0.05> PCT_Initial;

How bad is that to do? (The initial conditions should be nowhere near 5% infected.)
Alternatively, I can leave those alone and multiply the (0,1) bounded elements to constrain them when creating the vector (Uglier, but effective.)
Lastly, I could use a 3-simplex, and split the people. (If so, do I sample each element in the simplex independently? Is that legal?)

Any suggestions? Is there a best practice on this?
(I noticed that Andrew has said he prefers soft constraints in other contexts. I'm not sure that makes sense to me here, because the two values must sum to <=1, by definition.)

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestions re:Hard or Soft Constraints and using Narrow Ranges (for an ODE)?
parts:
If you want two values alpha and beta such that 0 < alpha + beta < 1,
then you can do this:

real<lower=0, upper=1> alpha;
real<lower=0, upper=(1 - alpha)> beta;

It's a stick-breaking process where alpha breaks off a piece
from (0,1) and then beta breaks off a piece of what's left.
It's the same construction our simplex constraint uses.
Stan takes care of the Jacobians for constrained variables,
so you can use the resulting variables without adjusting for
changes of variables.

- Bob

P.S. This kind of thing could cause numerical issues:

> PCT_Initial ~ beta(1,1000000);

It's going to put most of the prior mass very close to 0.
At least it's better than putting it close to 1 numerically.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Suggestions re:Hard or Soft Constraints and using Narrow Ranges (for an ODE)?
parts:
By scale-free do you mean roughly unit scaled in the unconstrained space?

That means if Y in (0, 1) is a random variable distributed

Y ~ beta(1, 1e6)

then

logit(Y) = log(Y / (1 - Y))

will has a density with mean -14 and sd 1.3.

I'm not sure how to do that change of variables.

I could change the model and use a unit normal prior on (logit(Y) / 1.3 + 14),
but that gives me a symmetric prior on the logit scale rather than the highly
skewed one you get for logit(Y) from Y ~ beta(1, 1d6).

- Bob

parts:
Hi, what I mean is that you don’t want a parameter with a value such as 1e-6. I don’t know the context here, but let me make something up. Suppose this parameter represents the rate of some rare disease in the population, something like spongiform or whatever. Then I think it should be rescaled. The lazy way would be to just rescale it as the rate per million people. Better would be to do some sort of natural scaling, I’m not quite sure how—it would depend on the context, perhaps the rate of people with the disease is the product of the rate of exposure times the rate of transmission, or whatever.

The point is to avoid parameters such as .000001 or 100000 or whatever.

A
